mean: surrounded by enemies on all sides
lit: songs of Chu heard on all four sides

story.text: Xiang Yu, king of Chu, was trapped at Gaixia by the Han army of Liu Bang. At night he heard the songs of Chu rising from the Han camps all around him and cried out in alarm: has Han already taken all of Chu? How many men of Chu they have! That night he drank in his tent and sang a lament naming his horse and his consort Yu; then he broke out with some eight hundred horsemen and died soon after at the Wu River.

use.how: Predicate, or in 陷入四面楚歌的境地: 公司四面楚歌。 Said of a person, team or business isolated and attacked from every side at once.

near.diff: 走投无路 is having no way out at all; 四面楚歌 stresses being isolated and pressed by opponents on every side.

cue: In one month a small shop gets new rivals on every side, its supplier drops it and its landlord raises the rent. How would you describe its position?

ctx.s: 那家小店前有大超市，后有网店，真是{四面楚歌}。
ctx.en: That little shop has a big supermarket on one side and online stores on the other; it's besieged on all sides.

ctx.s: 他得罪了老板，又跟同事闹翻，一下子陷入了{四面楚歌}的境地。
ctx.en: He offended the boss and fell out with his colleagues, and suddenly found himself surrounded by enemies.

ctx.s: 产品出了质量问题，投诉、退货、负面新闻一起涌来，公司{四面楚歌}。
ctx.en: The product had a quality problem; complaints, returns and bad press poured in all at once, and the company was beset on every side.

ctx.s: 球队连输几场，球迷骂、媒体批，主教练是不是已经{四面楚歌}了？
ctx.en: After a string of losses, with the fans cursing and the media attacking, isn't the head coach now besieged from all sides?

ctx.s: “你们组的方案还撑得住吗？”“撑不住了，各部门都反对，我们简直是{四面楚歌}。”
ctx.en: "Can your team's plan hold up?" "No. Every department opposes it; we're surrounded."

ctx.s: 到了小说结尾，主人公身边已无一人可信，{四面楚歌}，只好独自离开了那座城市。
ctx.en: By the end of the novel the hero has no one left he can trust, enemies on every side, and he leaves the city alone.

bad.s: 我们的新家四面都是山，风景很好，真是{四面楚歌}。
bad.en: (meant: our new home has mountains on all sides and lovely views)
bad.why: It means being besieged and isolated by opponents; it never describes pleasant surroundings.

bad.s: 生日那天朋友们围着我唱歌，我{四面楚歌}，特别开心。
bad.en: (meant: friends gathered round and sang to me on my birthday)
bad.why: The songs in the idiom are the enemy's; it describes a desperate, isolated position, not happy singing.

mean: an idyllic haven away from the world
lit: a peach-blossom spring outside the world

story.text: A fisherman of Wuling followed a stream lined with blossoming peach trees to its source, squeezed through a narrow opening in a hill and came out into a peaceful village of fields, ponds and houses. The villagers' ancestors had fled the wars of the Qin; they had never heard of the Han, let alone the Wei and Jin. They feasted him, and when he left he marked his way, yet no one could ever find the place again.

use.how: Noun, often after 是 or 像, or as 世外桃源般的: 这里简直是世外桃源。 Said of a quiet, lovely place cut off from the noise of the world, or of such a place as an unreal ideal.

near.diff: 人间天堂 is any very beautiful, rich place, even a busy city; 世外桃源 must be secluded and untouched by the outside world.

cue: After hours on mountain roads you reach a village with no phone signal, clear streams and old people farming as they always have. What do you call it?

ctx.s: 这个小山村没有汽车，也没有高楼，像一个{世外桃源}。
ctx.en: This little mountain village has no cars and no tall buildings; it's like a hidden paradise.

ctx.s: 退休以后，他在山里买了一座小院，过起了{世外桃源}般的生活。
ctx.en: After retiring he bought a small house in the mountains and began living a life apart from the world.

ctx.s: “这里连手机信号都没有？”“没有才好，简直是{世外桃源}。”
ctx.en: "There's not even phone signal here?" "All the better. It's a real haven from the world."

ctx.s: 城市里哪有什么{世外桃源}？想清静，就得学会给自己的心留一块地方。
ctx.en: Where in a city would you find a haven from the world? If you want peace, you have to learn to keep a quiet place in your own heart.

ctx.s: 湖心小岛与世隔绝，居民自给自足，被游客称为现代的{世外桃源}。
ctx.en: The island in the middle of the lake is cut off from the world and its people are self-sufficient; visitors call it a modern Shangri-La.

ctx.s: 他总想逃到一个没有烦恼的{世外桃源}去，可现实问题终究要面对。
ctx.en: He always wants to escape to some untroubled paradise, but sooner or later real problems have to be faced.

bad.s: 上海是个热闹繁华的{世外桃源}，到处都是高楼。
bad.en: (meant: Shanghai is a lively, prosperous paradise full of skyscrapers)
bad.why: It must be a secluded, quiet place cut off from the world; a busy, crowded city is the opposite.

bad.s: 我打算周末{世外桃源}一下，去郊区放松放松。
bad.en: (meant: I plan to get away from it all this weekend)
bad.why: It is a noun naming a place, not a verb meaning to get away from it all.

mean: to offer one's modest view to draw out better ones
lit: to toss out a brick in order to draw out jade

use.how: A modest phrase for one's own contribution, usually when speaking first: 我先说几句，算是抛砖引玉。 Not used to describe other people's input.

near.diff: 班门弄斧 is showing off in front of experts; 抛砖引玉 is offering one's rough view first so that others will offer better ones.

cue: At a meeting nobody wants to speak first, so you offer a rough idea and say you hope others will improve on it. What do you call your opening?

ctx.s: 我先说说我的想法，算是{抛砖引玉}，请大家多提意见。
ctx.en: Let me share my thoughts first, just to get things going; I hope everyone will chip in.

ctx.s: 这篇短文只是{抛砖引玉}，希望能引起更多老师对这个问题的讨论。
ctx.en: This short piece is only meant to start the conversation; I hope more teachers will take up the question.

ctx.s: 会议冷场了，组长只好先讲了一个不成熟的方案来{抛砖引玉}。
ctx.en: The meeting went silent, so the team leader put forward a half-formed plan to get others talking.

ctx.s: “你怎么第一个发言？”“总得有人{抛砖引玉}吧，不然大家都不开口。”
ctx.en: "Why did you speak first?" "Someone has to break the ice, or nobody says anything."

ctx.s: 主持人笑着说：“我先{抛砖引玉}，讲讲我第一次出国时闹的笑话。”
ctx.en: The host smiled: "I'll start us off by telling you about the blunders I made on my first trip abroad."

ctx.s: 本次讲座只介绍几种基本方法，意在{抛砖引玉}，深入的研究还有待各位。
ctx.en: This lecture only introduces a few basic methods, meant to prompt your own ideas; the deeper research is up to you.

bad.s: 专家的报告非常精彩，真是{抛砖引玉}。
bad.en: (meant: the expert's report was excellent)
bad.why: The brick is one's own modest offering; applied to someone else's excellent talk it calls their work a brick and sounds like a slight.

bad.s: 这道题太难了，我{抛砖引玉}了半天也没想出答案。
bad.en: (meant: I racked my brains for ages)
bad.why: It is not about thinking hard; it means offering your own view first so others will contribute theirs.

lit: the Jingwei bird filling up the sea

story.text: The youngest daughter of the Flame Emperor went to play on the Eastern Sea, drowned and never came back. She turned into a small bird called Jingwei, named for its cry, and ever since it has carried twigs and stones in its beak from the western mountains and dropped them into the Eastern Sea, trying to fill it up.

use.how: Predicate, or in 精卫填海的精神 / 像精卫填海一样. Praises stubborn effort at a task far too big for the one doing it; it can also hint that the task looks hopeless.

near.diff: 愚公移山 says patient effort over generations will finally win; 精卫填海 stresses a small creature's defiant will against a task that seems endless.

cue: A lone young woman picks plastic off the beach every morning, a handful at a time, though everyone says the ocean can never be cleaned. What spirit does she show?

ctx.s: 她一个人坚持清理河里的垃圾，像{精卫填海}一样从不放弃。
ctx.en: She keeps clearing rubbish from the river all on her own, never giving up, like the bird trying to fill the sea.

ctx.s: 面对一望无际的海洋垃圾，几个志愿者每天去捡，凭的就是一股{精卫填海}的精神。
ctx.en: Facing endless rubbish in the ocean, a few volunteers go out to pick it up every day, driven by a will that never yields to impossible odds.

ctx.s: 有人笑他们是{精卫填海}，白费力气，可他们还是一年年干了下去。
ctx.en: Some mocked them as trying to fill the sea, wasting their strength, but they kept at it year after year.

ctx.s: “就凭我们几个人，能改变什么？”“{精卫填海}也是一点一点填的，先做起来再说。”
ctx.en: "What can a few of us change?" "Even the bird filled the sea one stone at a time. Let's just start."

ctx.s: 她失去孩子后，一个人四处奔走推动水上安全教育，这份{精卫填海}般的执着让人感动。
ctx.en: After losing her child she campaigned alone everywhere for water-safety education; her dogged, defiant persistence is moving.

ctx.s: 文章写道，山区教师用一生守护孩子们的读书梦，正是{精卫填海}的写照。
ctx.en: The article says that mountain-village teachers who give their lives to the children's hopes of schooling embody that unyielding spirit.

bad.s: 他熬夜一个小时就把作业写完了，真是{精卫填海}。
bad.en: (meant: he stayed up an hour and got his homework done)
bad.why: It describes long, stubborn effort against an overwhelming task, not finishing a small job quickly.

bad.s: 孩子们在海边用沙子{精卫填海}，玩得很开心。
bad.en: (meant: the children had fun throwing sand into the sea)
bad.why: It is a figure of heroic determination, not a description of literally tossing things into the sea for fun.

mean: so interdependent that one's loss endangers the other
lit: when the lips are gone, the teeth are cold

story.text: The state of Jin asked the small state of Yu to let its army pass through to attack the neighbouring state of Guo. Yu's minister Gong Zhiqi warned his duke that Yu and Guo protected each other: as the saying goes, when the lips are gone the teeth are cold. The duke would not listen and let the army through. Jin destroyed Guo, and on its way home it took Yu as well.

use.how: Predicate, or in 唇亡齿寒的道理/关系: 两家企业唇亡齿寒。 Said of two parties whose fates are so linked that the fall of one exposes the other; often a warning.

near.diff: 息息相关 is any close connection; 唇亡齿寒 warns specifically that one party's ruin will directly endanger the other.

cue: A parts supplier is going bankrupt, and the factory that depends on it realises it must help, or it will be next. Which idiom explains why?

ctx.s: 隔壁的书店关门了，我们咖啡馆的客人也少了，这就叫{唇亡齿寒}。
ctx.en: The bookshop next door closed and our café lost customers too; when one goes down, the other suffers.

ctx.s: 上游供应商要是倒了，我们工厂也撑不住，{唇亡齿寒}啊。
ctx.en: If our upstream supplier collapses, our factory can't survive either; our fates are tied together.

ctx.s: 两个村共用一道河堤，上村一旦决口，下村也保不住，{唇亡齿寒}，修堤必须一起出力。
ctx.en: The two villages share one dyke; if it breaks at the upper village, the lower one is lost too. Their fates are linked, so they must repair it together.

ctx.s: “别人家出事，跟我们有什么关系？”“怎么没关系？{唇亡齿寒}的道理你不懂吗？”
ctx.en: "What does their trouble have to do with us?" "Everything! Don't you see that if they fall, we're exposed?"

ctx.s: 文章指出，旅游业一旦垮掉，当地餐馆也会跟着关门，两者{唇亡齿寒}。
ctx.en: The article points out that if tourism collapses, the local restaurants will close too; the two stand or fall together.

ctx.s: 古时候，相邻的小国往往{唇亡齿寒}，一国被灭，邻国也难以自保。
ctx.en: In ancient times neighbouring small states often depended on each other; when one was destroyed, the next could hardly defend itself.

bad.s: 冬天我嘴唇干裂，牙齿也怕冷，真是{唇亡齿寒}。
bad.en: (meant: in winter my lips crack and my teeth are sensitive to cold)
bad.why: It is a figure for two parties whose fates are linked, never a description of chapped lips or cold teeth.

bad.s: 他们俩{唇亡齿寒}，天天吵架，谁也不理谁。
bad.en: (meant: the two of them are always at odds)
bad.why: It describes interdependence, where one's fall hurts the other, not a quarrelsome relationship.

mean: a rare friend who truly understands one

story.text: Bo Ya was a master of the qin, and Zhong Ziqi was the listener who truly heard him. When Bo Ya played with high mountains in mind, Ziqi said: lofty, like Mount Tai! When he played thinking of flowing water, Ziqi said: vast, like the great rivers! Whatever Bo Ya meant, Ziqi understood. When Ziqi died, Bo Ya broke his qin, cut its strings and never played again, feeling no one left was worth playing for.

use.how: Noun or modifier, often 高山流水的知音 or 高山流水遇知音. Said of a deep friendship of minds, especially over art; it can also praise refined music.

near.diff: 志同道合 is sharing the same goals or ideals; 高山流水 is the rarer bond of someone who understands one's inner thoughts and art.

cue: A composer writes for years unnoticed, until one listener describes exactly what each piece was meant to say. What kind of bond have they found?

ctx.s: 他们俩一个弹琴一个听，彼此最懂对方，真是{高山流水}的知音。
ctx.en: One plays and the other listens; they understand each other completely, true kindred spirits.

ctx.s: 她写的诗很少有人懂，直到遇见他，才算是{高山流水}遇知音。
ctx.en: Few people understood her poems until she met him; at last she had found the one who truly understood.

ctx.s: “你们俩认识这么多年，靠什么维持友谊？”“说不上来，就是一种{高山流水}的默契吧。”
ctx.en: "You've known each other for years; what keeps the friendship going?" "Hard to say. We just understand each other without words."

ctx.s: 人这一生，能遇到一位{高山流水}般的朋友，已经很幸运了。
ctx.en: In a whole lifetime, meeting one friend who truly understands you is already great luck.

ctx.s: 这部电影讲述了两位老艺人之间{高山流水}般的友情。
ctx.en: The film tells of the rare, deep friendship between two old artists.

ctx.s: 音乐会上，钢琴家与小提琴手心意相通，琴声宛如{高山流水}。
ctx.en: At the concert the pianist and the violinist were perfectly attuned, and their music was sublime.

bad.s: 这里有{高山流水}，风景特别美，我们周末去爬山吧。
bad.en: (meant: there are tall mountains and streams here; let's go hiking)
bad.why: It is a figure for a soulmate friend or refined music, not a description of real mountain scenery.

bad.s: 他跟新同事很快就{高山流水}了。
bad.en: (meant: he quickly hit it off with his new colleague)
bad.why: It names a rare bond of understanding and works as a noun or modifier, not as a verb meaning to get along.

lit: the furnace flame has turned pure blue, the alchemist's sign that the work is done

use.how: Predicate, often 已经炉火纯青 or 达到炉火纯青的地步/境界: 他的厨艺炉火纯青。 Praises a skill brought to perfection by long practice.

near.diff: 游刃有余 is handling a task with ease and room to spare; 炉火纯青 is a skill itself brought to perfection over years.
出神入化 is skill so wonderful it seems magical; 炉火纯青 stresses mastery that has matured through long practice.

cue: After forty years at the same stall, the old noodle maker pulls dough thinner than thread without even looking. How would you describe his craft?

ctx.s: 王师傅做了三十年面条，手艺已经{炉火纯青}。
ctx.en: Master Wang has made noodles for thirty years; his craft is perfected.

ctx.s: 她的书法练到了{炉火纯青}的地步，一笔一画都很有功力。
ctx.en: Her calligraphy has reached a level of mastery; every stroke shows real skill.

ctx.s: “这道菜你怎么做得这么好吃？”“哪里，离{炉火纯青}还差得远呢。”
ctx.en: "How do you make this dish so delicious?" "Oh, I'm nowhere near mastering it yet."

ctx.s: 这位演员的表演已达{炉火纯青}的境界，每个眼神都恰到好处。
ctx.en: This actor's craft has reached perfection; every glance is exactly right.

ctx.s: 一个刚入门的新手，凭什么说自己的技术已经{炉火纯青}了？
ctx.en: How can a beginner who has only just started claim his technique is already perfected?

ctx.s: 这位老焊工干了一辈子，焊缝又细又匀，技术可谓{炉火纯青}。
ctx.en: This old welder has done the job all his life; his seams are fine and even, and his skill can truly be called consummate.

bad.s: 我刚学了一个月钢琴，弹得{炉火纯青}。
bad.en: (meant: after a month of piano lessons I play very well)
bad.why: It praises mastery reached through many years of practice; a month of lessons makes the claim absurd.

bad.s: 厨房里{炉火纯青}，火烧得很旺，我们快开饭了。
bad.en: (meant: the stove is burning hot and dinner is nearly ready)
bad.why: It is a figure for perfected skill, not a description of a real stove fire.

use.how: Predicate, often after 是 or 如: 这样的人才凤毛麟角。 Says something precious, especially talent, is extremely rare; not used of rare bad things.

near.diff: 寥寥无几 is a plain 'very few', of anything; 凤毛麟角 implies the few are precious and valuable.
屈指可数 says the number is small enough to count on one's fingers; 凤毛麟角 stresses rarity and preciousness.

cue: The firm interviewed hundreds of people, and only one could both write code and speak three languages well. How rare are such candidates?

ctx.s: 既懂技术又会管理的人才，在我们公司是{凤毛麟角}。
ctx.en: People who understand the technology and can also manage are extremely rare in our company.

ctx.s: 在那个年代，能读上大学的女孩子如{凤毛麟角}。
ctx.en: In those days, girls who got to go to university were extremely rare.

ctx.s: “现在还有会修古董钟表的老师傅吗？”“有，不过已经是{凤毛麟角}了。”
ctx.en: "Are there still craftsmen who can repair antique clocks?" "There are, but they're precious few now."

ctx.s: 能把古琴弹得这么好的年轻人，可谓{凤毛麟角}。
ctx.en: Young people who can play the guqin this well are rare indeed.

ctx.s: 研究这种古文字的学者本来就{凤毛麟角}，能读懂原文的更少。
ctx.en: Scholars of this ancient script are rare to begin with, and those who can read the originals are rarer still.

ctx.s: 他翻遍了旧书店，像这样保存完好的初版书简直是{凤毛麟角}。
ctx.en: He searched every second-hand bookshop; a first edition preserved this well is a rare treasure.

bad.s: 我们班上逃课的学生{凤毛麟角}，大家都很守纪律。
bad.en: (meant: hardly anyone in our class skips lessons)
bad.why: It implies the rare things are precious, so it reads as praising truants; a plain word for 'very few' is needed.

bad.s: 他是一个{凤毛麟角}的人，长得很奇怪。
bad.en: (meant: he is an odd-looking person)
bad.why: It speaks of preciousness and rarity, not of strange appearance.

mean: vast changes over the course of time
lit: the blue sea turns into mulberry fields

story.text: The immortal Magu, meeting the immortal Wang Fangping, told him that she had already seen the Eastern Sea turn into mulberry fields three times. On her recent visit to Penglai, she said, the water was only about half as deep as at their last meeting; perhaps it was about to become dry land again.

use.how: Predicate, subject or object of 经历/历经: 几十年沧海桑田。 Said of great changes in the world or a place over a long time, often with a sigh.

near.diff: 物是人非 is the sadness that places remain while the people are gone; 沧海桑田 is the world itself transformed over time.
日新月异 praises rapid, continuing progress; 沧海桑田 is vast change seen over a long span, often with a sigh.

cue: An old man returns to the fishing village of his childhood and finds the bay filled in and covered with towers. What does he sigh?

ctx.s: 小时候这里还是一片海，现在全是高楼，真是{沧海桑田}。
ctx.en: When I was a child this was all sea; now it's all high-rises. How the world changes.

ctx.s: 几十年过去，世间经历了{沧海桑田}，老两口的感情依旧没变。
ctx.en: Decades passed and the world changed beyond recognition, but the old couple's love stayed the same.

ctx.s: “这条街以前是什么样的？”“说来话长，{沧海桑田}，早就不是原来的样子了。”
ctx.en: "What was this street like before?" "That's a long story. Everything has changed; it's nothing like it was."

ctx.s: 地质学家告诉我们，这片高原曾经是海底，{沧海桑田}并不只是传说。
ctx.en: Geologists tell us this plateau was once the seabed; seas becoming land is not just a legend.

ctx.s: 读这本家族史，一百年的{沧海桑田}尽在其中。
ctx.en: Reading this family history, you see a whole century of upheaval and change.

ctx.s: 世事{沧海桑田}，谁能想到当年的荒滩会变成今天的新城？
ctx.en: The world changes beyond all recognition; who could have imagined the barren shore of those days becoming today's new city?

bad.s: 我昨天剪了头发，变化很大，真是{沧海桑田}。
bad.en: (meant: I had a haircut yesterday and look very different)
bad.why: It speaks of vast change over long years; using it for an overnight personal change sounds ridiculous.

bad.s: 海边有一片{沧海桑田}，农民在那里种桑树。
bad.en: (meant: by the sea there are fields where farmers grow mulberry)
bad.why: It is a figure for great change over time, not a description of real fields by the sea.

lit: wherever it heads, everything bends flat, like grass before the wind

use.how: Predicate, often 一路所向披靡: 这支球队所向披靡。 Said of an army, team, player or product that overwhelms every opponent it meets.

near.diff: 势如破竹 stresses unstoppable momentum once an advance begins; 所向披靡 stresses that every opponent falls before it.
所向无敌 says no one can match it; 所向披靡 adds the picture of opponents giving way in rout.

cue: A newcomer boxer knocks out every opponent in the tournament, one after another, without losing a single round. How did he go through the field?

ctx.s: 这支球队今年{所向披靡}，一场都没输过。
ctx.en: This team has swept all before it this year and hasn't lost a single game.

ctx.s: 小组赛里，她{所向披靡}，轻松进入了决赛。
ctx.en: In the group stage she crushed every opponent and reached the final with ease.

ctx.s: “你觉得他们能拿冠军吗？”“看他们一路{所向披靡}的势头，很有希望。”
ctx.en: "Do you think they can win the title?" "The way they've flattened everyone so far, I'd say there's a good chance."

ctx.s: 小说里的这位将军{所向披靡}，最后却败给了自己的傲慢。
ctx.en: The general in the novel defeats every enemy, but in the end is undone by his own arrogance.

ctx.s: 这款手机上市后{所向披靡}，几个月就占领了大半个市场。
ctx.en: After launch this phone swept aside its rivals and took most of the market within months.

ctx.s: 再{所向披靡}的队伍，也会有输球的一天，不是吗？
ctx.en: Even a team that crushes everyone will lose a game someday, won't it?

bad.s: 我们队昨天{所向披靡}，以零比五输给了对手。
bad.en: (meant: our team was routed yesterday, losing five-nil)
bad.why: It means crushing every opponent; it cannot describe one's own heavy defeat.

bad.s: 风很大，路边的小草{所向披靡}。
bad.en: (meant: the wind was strong and the grass by the road was flattened)
bad.why: Though the image is grass bent by wind, the idiom only describes an overwhelming force, not real grass.
